title: Lesson 8: The Grace and Mercy Cycle
description: Four words explain what God did for you at the cross: Grace, Mercy, Justified, and Righteous. Through an interactive diagram you will build step by step, you will see how these four realities work together in a cycle that starts with God's love and flows through you to others.

blocks.text: In the last lesson, you learned how to study the Bible for yourself, observing what the text says, interpreting what it means, and applying it to your life. You walked through Psalm 23 with the Shepherd's voice in your ears. Now you turn from learning how to read God's Word to looking again at what God has actually done for you at the cross.

For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them.

Paul says three things that will reshape how you understand everything God has done for you. First, salvation is a gift. You did not earn it. Second, it came by grace through faith, not by anything you did. Third, God did not save you so you could sit still. He saved you so that His grace would flow through you and into the lives of the people around you.

This lesson is built around four words that every believer should know: Grace, Mercy, Justified, and Righteous. These are big church words, but they describe something so simple and so good that once you see it, you will never forget it.
Four Words That Change Everything

Grace means getting a gift you do not deserve. You did nothing to earn it, and you could never pay it back. Mercy means not getting the punishment you do deserve. You broke the law, you earned the sentence, but the judge does not punish you. Justified means your punishment has been paid. Someone else stepped in and settled your debt. Righteous means you are now seen as perfect before God, not because you became perfect overnight, but because Jesus' perfect life was placed on your account.
Put those four together and you have the whole story of what happened to you at the cross. Before opening the diagram, picture it like this.

blocks.alt: A king showing mercy to a kneeling servant whose impossible debt has been forgiven

blocks.title: The Unmerciful Servant
blocks.text:
Jesus once told a story about a servant who owed his king more than he could ever pay back. One day the king ordered the debt to be repaid in full. Since the servant could not pay, the king ordered that the servant, his family, and everything he owned be sold to begin paying the debt. The man fell on his knees and begged for mercy.

But the king did more than give him more time. Out of pity, he released him and forgave the whole debt. Not a payment plan. Not a reduced amount. The entire impossible debt was gone.

Then that same servant walked out and found another servant who owed him a much smaller amount. He grabbed him, demanded payment, ignored the same plea for patience, and had him thrown into prison. When the king heard, he called the servant back and asked, "Should not you have had mercy on your fellow servant, as I had mercy on you?" (Matthew 18:33). The king's servant was covered in mercy but refused to let that mercy move through him.

Jesus' parable puts mercy and forgiven debt in front of you first. The servant's problem was not that he misunderstood the king's mercy. He received it. His problem was that mercy stopped with him. Jesus is showing us that canceled debt is meant to turn debtors into merciful people.
8.1 - In Jesus' parable, what stands out to you most about the king's mercy and the servant's response?

Walking Through the Five Steps

Step 1: Mercy. In Jesus' parable, the king does not give the servant the punishment his debt deserves. He has compassion and releases him. In the same way, God looked at your sin and had every right to condemn you. Instead, He responded with compassion. Mercy is not getting the punishment you do deserve.

Step 2: Justified. The servant's debt was not small, and your sin is not small either. A holy God cannot pretend evil does not matter. At the cross, Jesus stepped into your place and paid what you could never pay. God's mercy is not casual; it is just, because Jesus bore the cost. Justified means your punishment is paid in full, and it is "Just-if-I'd" never sinned.

Step 3: Righteous. Jesus' parable shows a debt forgiven. The gospel goes even further. God does not only remove your debt; He gives you the perfect life of Jesus as your standing before Him. The perfect life that Jesus lived is the very life that God sees when He looks at you. The "Great Exchange" is that Jesus takes the punishment for your sin and gives you His perfection.
For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.

Step 4: Grace. The servant walked out free because the king gave him a gift he could never deserve. In Christ, God gives even more. He does not only release you from punishment. He gives you salvation, adoption, new life, and good works prepared for you to walk in. That is grace. You get a gift you do not deserve.
For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast.

Step 5: The Grace and Mercy Cycle. This is where Jesus' parable presses hardest. The forgiven servant should have become a forgiving servant. The mercy he received should have shaped the mercy he gave. This is how the cycle works. Consider the diagram: when the arrow reaches Grace, it does not stop. It points back toward Mercy. Those who have received mercy become people who show mercy. Those who have been given grace become people who give grace.
Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you.
8.2 - As you walked through The Grace and Mercy Cycle, which part helped you better understand the grace and mercy of Jesus toward you, and why?
The Mercy That Moves Through You

Jesus' parable is not only a warning about hypocrisy. It is training in how grace moves. The king's question still lands: Should not you have had mercy, as I had mercy on you? Forgiveness does not mean the wrong was small. It means the mercy you received from God is now larger in your heart than the debt someone else owes you. At the cross, Jesus absorbed the true cost of sin so mercy could reach you without pretending justice did not matter. Now that same mercy starts moving outward. You are God's workmanship, made to do good works, forgive as you have been forgiven, and live as someone whose impossible debt has been canceled. That is the grace cycle.
8.3 - Who in your life needs you to show them the mercy or grace you have received from God? What would that look like this week?
Lesson 8 Review

Four words name what God did for you at the cross: Mercy, Justified, Righteous, and Grace. He withheld the punishment you earned, paid your debt in full through Jesus, gave you Christ's perfect life as your own standing, and handed you a gift you could never deserve. Then the cycle keeps going, just like Jesus warned in the parable of the unmerciful servant. The mercy and grace you have received are the very mercy and grace you now extend to others. In the next lesson you will see what it looks like when grace this big starts growing fruit through your daily life.
